old: Two large General-Practice-based trials (fractures n = 5451; serious fall injuries n = 9803) found NO significant reduction in falls or fractures — raises questions about funding/implementing interventions; multifactorial interventions work better when provided directly than when relying on referral to routine service providers (p641).
new: Two large primary-care trials found no significant reduction in their respective primary outcomes: fractures in PreFIT (9,803 participants) and serious fall injuries in STRIDE (5,451 participants). old: PLMS last 0.5 seconds to 10 seconds, 5 to 90 seconds apart; at least four in a row required; PLMD needs at least 15 PLMS/hour (p651).

old: Drugs (Table 44-2, p653): Ropinirole 0.25–4 mg, Pramipexole 0.125–2 mg — caution: augmentation, behavioral disinhibition. Carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg — reserve for infrequent dosing (highest augmentation risk). Gabapentin enacarbil 600–1200 mg (only α2δ ligand FDA-approved for RLS), gabapentin 100–1800 mg, pregabalin 300 mg — caution: sedation, suicidal ideation. Clonazepam 0.25–2 mg, temazepam 15–30 mg — limited evidence, cognitive risk. new: RLS drug selection. The AASM favors gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil and pregabalin when appropriate. FDA-labeled gabapentin enacarbil is 600 mg daily for RLS with normal renal function; 1,200 mg adds adverse effects without additional benefit. Dopamine agonists can cause augmentation and behavioral disinhibition. If pramipexole is chosen, the labeled RLS titration is 0.125–0.5 mg once daily. The labeled ropinirole range begins at 0.25 mg, up to 4 mg daily. Table 44-2 lists carbidopa/levodopa 25/100–25/200 mg for infrequent use because of augmentation. Table 44-2 lists off-label gabapentin 100–1,800 mg and pregabalin 300 mg as studied doses. Adjust for renal function and monitor sedation. The table lists clonazepam 0.25–2 mg and temazepam 15–30 mg, with limited evidence and cognitive/fall risks. Its off-label opioid examples are codeine 30–60 mg, tramadol 50–100 mg, oxycodone 5–15 mg, hydrocodone 5–15 mg and methadone 5–10 mg. These are historical table ranges. Specialist assessment of respiratory, dependence and medication risks is essential in refractory RLS (p653; FDA prescribing information for Horizant and pramipexole, AASM 2025 RLS/PLMD guideline).Current practice (not the book): FDA-labelled RLS dosing of pramipexole is 0.125 mg once daily 2–3 h before bedtime, titrated if needed to 0.25 then 0.5 mg; no evidence that 0.75 mg adds benefit — US prescribing information (pramipexole tablets, DailyMed), 2026; Current practice (not the book): AASM conditionally suggests against standard pramipexole, transdermal rotigotine or ropinirole use in adults with RLS because of augmentation with longer-term treatment; evidence certainty is moderate for pramipexole/ropinirole and low for rotigotine; patients prioritizing short-term symptom relief over long-term adverse effects may still choose these agents - AASM 2025, recommendations 12-14, p144

old: Tasimelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) approved only for non–24-hour sleep-wake rhythm disorder (p657).
new: Tasimelteon is an MT1/MT2 agonist approved for Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in adults and for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith–Magenis syndrome. The formulation for the latter depends on age (p657; FDA Hetlioz prescribing information).

old: Chronic if symptoms persist more than 3 months; short-term if fewer than 3 months (p657).
new: Chronic insomnia causes sleep difficulty despite adequate opportunity, with daytime consequences, at least 3 nights/week for at least 3 months. Short-term insomnia lasts less than 3 months (p657; ICSD-3-TR, VA/DoD 2025 guideline, Appendix F).

old: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant/lemborexant (DORA) — only suvorexant FDA-approved for insomnia with Alzheimer dementia (trial of 277 patients, mild-moderate AD, sleep time up around half an hour after 2 weeks) (p660). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).
new: Drugs: Benzodiazepines ↓ sleep latency ~10 minutes, ↑ total sleep time 30 to 60 minutes; avoid long-acting flurazepam/quazepam; all Beers-listed (p659). Temazepam start 7.5 mg, usual 7.5–30 mg, half-life 8.8 h — caution: psychomotor impairment, increased fall risk; eszopiclone start 1 mg, usual 1–2 mg, half-life 6 h — caution: avoid high-fat meals, unpleasant taste/headache (Table 44-5, p660). Zolpidem/zaleplon — rapid onset, take immediately before bed; Beers-listed (p659). Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) — few side effects; lack of amnestic properties makes it somewhat less effective for subjective improvement in sleep (p660). Suvorexant and lemborexant are dual orexin receptor antagonists for insomnia. The suvorexant trial in mild–moderate probable Alzheimer dementia randomized 285, of whom 277 completed. Placebo-adjusted total sleep time improved by 28 minutes at week 4 (p660; Herring et al., FDA Belsomra prescribing information). Doxepin low-dose 3–6 mg for insomnia vs 100–300 mg as an antidepressant (p661). Avoid diphenhydramine as primary therapy — long half-life, next-day sedation, rapid tolerance, dry mouth, urinary retention, delirium, decreased cognition (p661).

old: AHI greater than 15 is diagnostic alone (or greater than 5 with significant symptoms/comorbidities); AHI greater than 30 is severe (p645).
new: At least 15 obstructive respiratory events/hour suffice, or at least 5/hour with relevant symptoms or comorbidities. An AHI of 30/hour or more is severe (p645; ICSD-3-TR).

old: EF less than 45% — the SERVE-HF trial found increased mortality with ASV in this group (p649).
new: LVEF ≤45% in symptomatic chronic heart failure with predominantly central sleep apnea. SERVE-HF found higher mortality with its ASV device in this population. The AASM limits consideration of ASV for central apnea in HFrEF to experienced centers with shared decision-making and close follow-up (p649). AASM 2025, recommendation 4

old: Episodic dizziness timing clue: <1 minute suggests BPPV; 20 to 120 minutes suggests TIA or migraine; >120 minutes to 2 days suggests Meniere disease/recurrent vestibulopathy (p670)
new: Episode duration is a clue. BPPV typically causes positional attacks lasting less than 1 minute. Spontaneous attacks can overlap in TIA, vestibular migraine and Ménière disease. Definite Ménière disease includes attacks lasting 20 minutes–12 hours with characteristic auditory findings; probable episodes can last up to 24 hours (p670; Bárány Society criteria).

old: ICD indicated for syncope + VT with EF <35%, syncope + prior MI, or VT induced on electrophysiologic study (p675)
new: Syncope caused by sustained VT warrants electrophysiologic assessment for an ICD, including ventricular function and reversible causes. After a previous MI, unexplained syncope with inducible sustained VT on electrophysiologic study is an ICD indication. Previous MI alone does not justify implantation (p675; ESC syncope guideline).

old: Drug doses for severe OH/PPH: caffeine 250 mg (2 cups brewed) each morning, fludrocortisone 0.1–0.5 mg po daily, midodrine 2.5–10 mg po TID, octreotide 50 mg subQ 30 min pre-meal (unusually high vs. the mcg doses typically used clinically — this is the book's own printed text) (p675)Current practice (not the book): the source trial gave octreotide 50 micrograms (µg) subQ, not 50 mg — Jansen et al., 1989 (PubMed 2646315).
new: For severe symptomatic OH, specialist options include midodrine 2.5–10 mg up to three times daily while awake (avoid near bedtime) or fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg daily with potassium, edema and supine BP monitoring. Avoid fludrocortisone in heart failure. For postprandial hypotension, the chapter discusses caffeine 250 mg in the morning and a small study of subcutaneous octreotide 50 micrograms before a glucose load (p675; OH review, AHA statement).Octreotide was studied in micrograms. The textbook’s milligram unit overstates the trial dose by a factor of 1,000 (Jansen et al., 1989).

old: Episodes lasting <1 minute suggest BPPV; 20 to 120 minutes suggest TIA or migraine; more than 120 minutes up to 2 days suggest Meniere disease or recurrent vestibulopathy (p670).
new: BPPV commonly causes positional spells under 1 minute. TIA and vestibular migraine can overlap in duration. Definite Ménière attacks last 20 minutes–12 hours with characteristic auditory findings, and probable attacks can last up to 24 hours (p670; Bárány Society criteria, PMID 25882471).

old: Blanchable erythema = discoloration >1cm (p686).
new: Blanchable erythema pales with gentle pressure and the color returns on release. The chapter describes a flat patch larger than 1 cm (p686). Size alone does not determine blanchability.

old: PUSH tool: 10 wound-size categories, exudate 0–3, tissue type 0–4 (p689).
new: PUSH scores wound area 0–10 (zero for a closed wound plus ten positive-size bands), exudate 0–3, and tissue type 0–4 (p689; NPIAP PUSH Tool 3.0).

old: Saline/water lack antiseptic properties and should seldom be used on (colonized) PI — antiseptic options: Dakin's 0.25% or povidone-iodine (10%/1% free iodine) on colonized PI, applied 10–15 min before redressing; lavage 4–15 psi (p692). For clean wounds, less force and physiologic solutions such as normal saline can be used (p693); avoid povidone-iodine, iodophor, sodium hypochlorite, hydrogen peroxide, and acetic acid on clean and healing PI (p697).
new: Clean a pressure injury with a nonirritating, nontoxic solution such as saline or clean water. Wound colonization alone does not justify routine antiseptics. If an antimicrobial cleanser is specifically indicated, select the agent, concentration and contact time for the wound and product. Historical examples include 0.25% sodium hypochlorite and 10% povidone-iodine containing 1% available iodine. Irrigation at 4–15 psi can remove debris. Avoid cytotoxic antiseptics on clean granulating tissue (pp692–693, 697; WHS guideline).

old: Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) 25–50 mg qd (p712) — beta-3 agonists should not be used in uncontrolled hypertension (p714).
new: Mirabegron 25–50 mg once daily for overactive bladder, with renal/hepatic dose adjustment when appropriate. Monitor BP. US labeling advises against mirabegron in severe uncontrolled hypertension (systolic ≥180 or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg). This warning is drug-specific (pp712,714; FDA mirabegron prescribing information).

old: Constipation is technically < 3 bowel movements/week (p717); the most common causes of fecal incontinence are constipation and laxative use, neurologic disorders, and colorectal disorders (p716); relieving a fecal impaction can resolve urinary as well as fecal incontinence (p701).
new: Fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements/week is one feature of constipation. Hard stool, straining or incomplete evacuation can occur even with daily bowel movements (p717). Common contributors to fecal incontinence include constipation/impaction, laxative use, and neurologic or colorectal disorders (p716). Relieving impaction can improve both urinary and fecal incontinence (p701).

old: EWGSOP2: assess strength first when sarcopenia is suspected; use muscle mass to confirm a muscular contribution to weakness. The book calls low strength without a mass measurement “suspected sarcopenia.” Muscle quality may substitute for mass; low physical performance indicates severity and greater adverse-outcome risk. Case finding uses symptoms or questionnaires (p732).
new: EWGSOP2: assess strength first when sarcopenia is suspected; use muscle mass to confirm a muscular contribution to weakness. Low strength is probable sarcopenia in EWGSOP2. Hazzard uses “suspected” for this stage before muscle quantity or quality is measured. Muscle quality may substitute for mass; low physical performance indicates severity and greater adverse-outcome risk. Case finding uses symptoms or questionnaires (p732; EWGSOP2 consensus).

old: The book reports high sensitivity at a low cutoff >1 point and good specificity at a high cutoff >4. Preserve those printed inequalities. Screening has not been proved cost-effective, universally or in selected settings/populations. SARC-F can help in settings with a high expected prevalence, including geriatric clinics, hospital, rehabilitation, and nursing homes; modified versions may add calf circumference (p734).
new: The book reports high sensitivity at a low cutoff >1 point and good specificity at a high cutoff >4. These are thresholds compared in the chapter. The usual positive SARC-F screen is ≥4/10 (p771). Screening has not been proved cost-effective, universally or in selected settings/populations. SARC-F can help in settings with a high expected prevalence, including geriatric clinics, hospital, rehabilitation, and nursing homes; modified versions may add calf circumference (p734).

old: Strength first; muscle mass or quality supports confirmation; low physical performance indicates severity.
new: In EWGSOP2, low strength indicates probable sarcopenia. Low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and low physical performance indicates severity.

old: The book calls low strength without mass measurement “suspected sarcopenia” (p732).
new: Hazzard calls the probable stage “suspected” (p732; EWGSOP2 consensus).

old: High sensitivity with a cutoff >1 point; good specificity with a cutoff >4.
new: The chapter reports high sensitivity above 1 point and good specificity above 4 when comparing thresholds (p734). The usual positive SARC-F screen is 4/10 or higher (p771).

old: Screening cost-effectiveness has not been established (p734).
new: Screening cost-effectiveness has not been established.

old: T-score > −1 = normal; ≤ −1 to > −2.5 = osteopenia (the table prints "≤ 1 but > −2.5" — minus sign evidently dropped); ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis; ≤ −2.5 + a fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis (p760).
new: DXA T-score ≥−1.0 is normal, below −1.0 but above −2.5 is low bone mass, and ≤−2.5 is osteoporosis. A T-score ≤−2.5 plus a fragility fracture defines severe/established osteoporosis in the WHO classification (Table 51-1, p760; Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation).

old: Trabecular bone = 80% of skeletal mass, more metabolically active than cortical bone (p760).
new: Cortical bone accounts for approximately 80% of total adult skeletal mass and trabecular bone for approximately 20%. Trabecular bone has higher metabolic activity and is prominent in the vertebrae and pelvis (p760; WHO Technical Report Series 921, correcting the mass attribution).

old: Calcium 1200–1500 mg/day; vitamin D ≥800 IU/day, though as much as 2000 IU/day and more may be needed to reach 25(OH)D ≥75 nmol/L (p772).
new: Hazzard discusses total elemental calcium 1,200–1,500 mg/day and vitamin D at least 800 IU/day, sometimes 2,000 IU/day or more to reach a bone-disease target of 75 nmol/L (30 ng/mL) (p772). Current BHOF calcium targets from diet plus supplements are 1,200 mg/day for women ≥51 and men ≥71 and 1,000 mg/day for men 50–70. Individualize supplementation and avoid exceeding the total target through unnecessary tablets (BHOF calcium and vitamin D).

old: Alendronate 70 mg weekly PO: ~50% ↓ hip + vertebral fracture over 3 years (Table 51-5, p774); equally effective ≤75 vs >75 years (51% vs 38% vertebral fracture reduction at 12 months); time to benefit 8 months (p775); contraindicated if eGFR < 35 mL/min (Table 51-5, p774).
new: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly reduced hip and vertebral fracture risk by roughly 50% over three years in the studies summarized (Table 51-5, p774). The cited age subgroups ≤75 and >75 had 51% and 38% lower vertebral fracture risk at 12 months, respectively. Estimated time to benefit in those ≥70 was 8 months (p775). US labeling does not recommend alendronate at creatinine clearance <35 mL/min. Contraindications to oral use include delayed esophageal emptying, inability to remain upright for 30 minutes and hypocalcemia (FDA Fosamax prescribing information).

old: Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly ×3: 70% ↓ vertebral, 25% ↓ nonvertebral, 41% ↓ hip fracture (p775); also cut all-cause mortality (9.6% vs 13% placebo) (p776).
new: Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly for three years reduced vertebral, nonvertebral and hip fracture risk by 70%, 25% and 41%, respectively, in the postmenopausal osteoporosis trial (p775). A separate trial in patients treated after hip-fracture repair reported deaths in 9.6% with zoledronic acid versus 13.3% with placebo (p776; HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial). US labeling contraindicates the osteoporosis infusion in acute renal impairment or creatinine clearance <35 mL/min.

old: Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months (dose per Table 51-5, p774 — the chapter's own prose on p776 prints "60 μg," a book table-vs-text discrepancy, see chapter note): 40% ↓ hip, 68% ↓ vertebral, 20% ↓ nonvertebral fracture; antifracture effect declines to pretreatment levels 12 months after stopping, and fracture risk rises markedly in those with prior vertebral fracture (p776).
new: Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months (dose per Table 51-5, p774 — the chapter's own prose on p776 prints "60 μg," a book table-vs-text discrepancy, see chapter note): 40% ↓ hip, 68% ↓ vertebral, 20% ↓ nonvertebral fracture; antifracture effect declines to pretreatment levels 12 months after stopping, and fracture risk rises markedly in those with prior vertebral fracture (p776). Plan antiresorptive follow-on before stopping or delaying treatment. Advanced CKD, particularly dialysis or CKD–mineral and bone disorder, raises the risk of severe hypocalcemia (FDA boxed warning).

old: Teriparatide 20 mcg/day SC, max 24 months: 65% ↓ vertebral, 53% ↓ nonvertebral fracture (p776); caution or avoidance if at increased osteosarcoma risk — Paget disease, previous radiation therapy, hypercalcemia, skeletal metastases, or history of prostate cancer/lymphoma (Table 51-5, p774).
new: Teriparatide 20 micrograms SC daily reduced vertebral and nonvertebral fractures by 65% and 53%, respectively, in the cited trial (pp774,776). US labeling permits treatment beyond two years only if high fracture risk persists or returns. Avoid in people at increased baseline osteosarcoma risk, including Paget disease, bone metastases, prior skeletal malignancy or radiation involving the skeleton. Avoid in underlying hypercalcemic disorders as a separate precaution (FDA Forteo prescribing information).

old: Abaloparatide 80 mcg/day SC, max 2 years: 86% ↓ vertebral, 43% ↓ nonvertebral fracture (p777).
new: Abaloparatide 80 micrograms SC daily reduced new vertebral fractures by 86% and nonvertebral fractures by 43% in the overall 18-month trial. US labeling does not recommend use for more than two years in a lifetime (p777; FDA Tymlos prescribing information).

old: Romosozumab 210 mg monthly SC, max 12 months; 12 months of romosozumab followed by 12 months of denosumab: 75% ↓ vertebral fracture; vs alendronate: 48% ↓ vertebral, 19% ↓ nonvertebral, 38% ↓ hip (p777).
new: Romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly for 12 doses. In FRAME, romosozumab versus placebo for one year, followed by denosumab in both groups, reduced new vertebral fractures 75% at two years. In ARCH, romosozumab versus alendronate for one year, followed by alendronate in both groups, reduced vertebral, nonvertebral and hip fractures by 48%, 19% and 38%, respectively (p777). US labeling advises against starting within one year of MI or stroke and calls for individual cardiovascular risk assessment (FDA Evenity boxed warning).

old: AFF: 3.2–50 per 100,000 person-years on bisphosphonates; >100 per 100,000 with long-term use (p777); investigate groin/thigh pain with x-ray (fracture often precedes pain) (p776).
new: AFF: 3.2–50 per 100,000 person-years on bisphosphonates; >100 per 100,000 with long-term use (p777); new groin or thigh pain warrants femur imaging for an incomplete atypical fracture. Prodromal pain can precede a complete fracture by weeks or months (pp776–777; FDA bisphosphonate prescribing information).

old: All residents: vitamin D ≥800 IU/day + calcium 1200 mg/day; check 25(OH)D first (p778).
new: All residents: vitamin D ≥800 IU/day + total calcium 1200 mg/day from food and supplements as needed. Individualize in CKD or hypercalcemia and check 25(OH)D first (p778).

old: Elemental calcium 1200–1500 mg/day; vitamin D at least 800 IU/day (as much as 2000 IU/day and more may be needed); serum 25(OH)D ≥ 75 nmol/L is optimally effective for fall and fracture prevention (p772). (p767 separately suggests a goal of > 80 nmol/L.)
new: Hazzard’s osteoporosis regimen discusses elemental calcium 1,200–1,500 mg/day and vitamin D at least 800 IU/day, sometimes 2,000 IU/day or more for its 75 nmol/L bone-disease target (p772; p767 separately mentions above 80 nmol/L). BHOF advises 1,200 mg/day total calcium for women ≥51 and men ≥71, and 1,000 mg/day for men 50–70. A universal 25(OH)D target for preventing falls in otherwise healthy adults has not been established (BHOF Clinician’s Guide; Endocrine Society 2024).

old: Vertebral fracture −70%, nonvertebral −25%, hip −41%; it also reduced all-cause mortality (9.6% vs 13% with placebo) (p775–776).
new: In the postmenopausal osteoporosis trial, vertebral, nonvertebral and hip fractures fell 70%, 25% and 41%. In a separate post-hip-fracture trial, all-cause mortality was 9.6% versus 13.3% with placebo (pp775–776; PMID 17878149).

old: Teriparatide and abaloparatide: maximum 2 years.
new: US labeling permits teriparatide beyond two years only when high fracture risk persists or returns. Abaloparatide beyond two years in a lifetime is not recommended.

old: Romosozumab: maximum 12 months.
new: Romosozumab is limited to 12 monthly doses as the anabolic effect wanes, followed by an antiresorptive when indicated.

old: Limits relate to osteosarcoma risk seen in nonclinical/animal studies (teriparatide) and a cardiovascular event signal plus potential oncogenesis (romosozumab) (p776–777).
new: Its separate boxed warning advises against starting within one year of MI or stroke (pp776–777; FDA Forteo, Tymlos and Evenity labels).

old: 3.2 to 50 cases per 100,000 person-years (higher, >100 per 100,000, with long-term use); new groin or thigh pain should prompt an x-ray, since fracture often precedes pain (p776–777).
new: The reported AFF risk is 3.2–50 per 100,000 person-years, and may exceed 100 per 100,000 after long exposure. New groin or thigh pain can signal an incomplete fracture weeks or months before a complete fracture. Obtain femur imaging (pp776–777; FDA bisphosphonate prescribing information).

old: Acetaminophen: FDA-reduced maximum dose 3 g/day (p787).
new: Acetaminophen: the ACR/AF OA guideline uses a conservative 3 g/day maximum for regular treatment, with monitoring and lower limits when indicated. The FDA general adult ceiling across all products is 4 g in 24 hours. Follow the lower product- or patient-specific limit, especially with liver disease, low body weight or substantial alcohol exposure (p787; FDA, ACR/AF OA guideline).

old: Intra-articular glucocorticoid: pain relief up to 2 months; no more than 3 injections per 6-month period (p789).
new: Intra-articular glucocorticoids may relieve pain for up to 2 months. Hazzard discourages more than three injections in six months (p789). Repeat injections are individualized. EULAR describes a customary limit of 3–4 per joint per year, while acknowledging limited evidence for a precise safe frequency (EULAR intra-articular therapy recommendations, 2021).

old: No more than 3 injections within a 6-month period; pain relief typically lasts up to 2 months (p789).
new: Hazzard advises against more than three injections in six months and describes pain relief lasting up to two months (p789). EULAR cites a customary limit of 3–4 injections in the same joint per year, with limited evidence for a universal safe count.

old: Match rehabilitation to functional loss, ability to participate, endurance and home support. Acute rehabilitation requires at least 3 hours/day and at least two therapy disciplines. (p. 800)
new: Match rehabilitation to functional loss, endurance, ability to participate and home support. US Medicare inpatient rehabilitation generally requires 3 hours/day on at least 5 days/week, or 15 hours within 7 consecutive days in documented cases. At least two therapy disciplines are needed, including PT or OT (p800; CMS inpatient rehabilitation criteria).

old: Continue DVT prophylaxis for 21-31 days after surgery. Up to 50% of previously independent older adults may need walking aids at 1 year. (p. 801)
new: Hazzard gives 21–31 days of postoperative thromboprophylaxis; NICE recommends one month after fragility hip/proximal femur fracture when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk. Up to 50% of previously independent older adults may need walking aids at one year (p801; NICE NG89, recommendation 1.11.2).

old: Ability to participate for at least
new: In a US Medicare inpatient rehabilitation facility, generally

old: 3 hours/day
new: 3 hours/day on at least 5 days/week , or 15 hours in 7 consecutive days

old: , with at least two rehabilitation disciplines involved. (p. 800)
new: in documented cases. Multiple therapy disciplines are required, including PT or OT (p800; CMS inpatient rehabilitation criteria).

old: Inpatient rehab facility: at least 3 hours of therapy/day required, 24-hr nursing (p822).
new: US Medicare inpatient rehabilitation includes 24-hour rehabilitation nursing and generally 3 hours of therapy per day on at least 5 days/week, or 15 hours in 7 consecutive days in documented cases. Multiple therapy disciplines participate, including PT or OT (p822; CMS inpatient rehabilitation criteria).

old: PAD: walk-to-pain program needs ≥6 months for benefit (p830).
new: PAD with claudication: supervised exercise uses intermittent walking to moderate-to-maximum symptoms, alternating with rest. A standard program is 30–45 minutes of active exercise at least 3 times/week for at least 12 weeks; continue training thereafter. The six-month period described on p830 is not a minimum time to benefit (2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline).

old: An inpatient rehab facility requires a minimum of 3 hours of therapy daily; a skilled nursing facility has no required intensity or duration of therapy (p822).
new: A US Medicare inpatient rehabilitation facility generally provides 3 hours of therapy on at least 5 days/week, or 15 hours over 7 consecutive days in documented cases. A skilled nursing facility has no equivalent fixed session-intensity requirement (p822, CMS inpatient rehabilitation coverage criteria).

old: 10% of US HIV cases are in patients ≥50; with modern ART, progression to HIV dementia is rare (2-3%), but milder deficits occur in 50-60% (p876)
new: CDC reported that over half of people living with diagnosed HIV in the US were aged 50 or older at the end of 2021. Hazzard cites an older 10% figure and reports 2–3% progression to HIV-associated dementia with combination ART and 50–60% prevalence of milder cognitive deficits in the cohorts it reviews (p876).

old: Roughly what fraction of US HIV cases are in patients 50 or older, and how common is progression to HIV-associated dementia with modern antiretroviral therapy?
new: What proportion of people living with diagnosed HIV in the US were aged 50 or older in CDC's 2021 data, and how does the chapter distinguish dementia from milder cognitive deficits?

old: About 10% of US HIV cases are in patients 50+; progression to HIV-associated dementia is now rare (2-3%) with combination antiretroviral therapy, though milder cognitive deficits still occur in 50-60% (p876).
new: Over half were 50 or older at the end of 2021 in CDC surveillance. The chapter's treated cohorts had an estimated 2–3% progression to HIV-associated dementia, while milder cognitive deficits were more frequent (50–60%, p876).

old: Late-onset (sporadic) AD = >95% of all AD cases (p894); familial (younger-onset, <65y) AD = 1–5% (p897).
new: Late-onset AD accounts for more than 95% of cases in the chapter's estimate (p894). Familial AD accounts for 1–5% and is one cause of younger-onset AD. Younger-onset disease can also occur without a causative familial mutation (p897).

old: Aducanumab — FDA accelerated approval June 2021 (p911); anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody, FDA-labeled only for MCI due to AD and mild AD (not moderate-to-severe AD) (Table 59-7, p914). One trial: 22% reduced cognitive decline (CDR-SB) over 18 months; no statistically significant benefit in the other trial. ARIA-E/ARIA-H in 34–36% of high-dose patients, ~80% of those asymptomatic (p911).
new: Aducanumab received FDA accelerated approval in June 2021 after trials in MCI due to AD or mild AD dementia (p911, Table 59-7, p914). EMERGE found 22% less worsening on CDR-SB over 18 months. ENGAGE did not show significant benefit. In the pooled 10 mg/kg groups, 35.2% had ARIA-E, 41.3% had any ARIA-E or ARIA-H, and 75.8% of participants with any ARIA were asymptomatic (EMERGE/ENGAGE safety analysis, Tables 1 and 3).

old: ARIA-E/ARIA-H occurred in 34–36% of high-dose patients; about 80% of those were asymptomatic (p911).
new: Of 1,029 high-dose participants, 425 (41.3%) had ARIA-E or ARIA-H, including 362 (35.2%) with ARIA-E. Among the 425 with any ARIA, 103 (24.2%) had symptoms and 322 (75.8%) did not (p911, EMERGE/ENGAGE integrated safety analysis, Tables 1 and 3).

old: Delirium-related agitation (short-term, low-dose), all q6h PRN: haloperidol 0.25–0.5 mg PO/IV, quetiapine 12.5–25 mg PO, olanzapine 2.5 mg PO or 1.25–2.5 mg IM, or risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg PO/IV (p923).Current practice (not the book): risperidone is not given IV; Risperdal Consta is IM only — "Do not administer intravenously" — Risperdal Consta prescribing information (Janssen).
new: For significant delirium-related agitation requiring short-term medication, the chapter gives these low PRN doses at six-hour intervals (p923). Haloperidol 0.25–0.5 mg orally (IV only with appropriate monitoring), quetiapine 12.5–25 mg orally, olanzapine 2.5 mg orally or 1.25–2.5 mg IM, or risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg orally. There is no approved IV risperidone formulation.Current practice (not the book): risperidone is not given IV; Risperdal Consta is IM only — "Do not administer intravenously" — Risperdal Consta prescribing information (Janssen).

old: PDD vs DLB "1-year rule": motor symptoms precede cognitive symptoms by >1 year in PDD; motor and cognitive symptoms arise within the same year in DLB (p939).
new: PDD: dementia begins more than one year after established motor parkinsonism. DLB: dementia begins before parkinsonism, together with it, or within one year after motor onset (p939, DLB Consortium 2017).

old: Amantadine — usually 100 mg BID for PD symptoms, usually 300–400 mg/day for antidyskinetic effect; confusion, hallucinations, livedo reticularis; often poorly tolerated in older adults (p944). Only established effective antidyskinetic agent (antiglutamatergic).
new: Amantadine, immediate release. The chapter describes 100 mg twice daily for motor symptoms and higher doses for dyskinesia (p944). In older adults, reduced renal clearance may cause accumulation. Use renal-function-adjusted dosing and monitor confusion, hallucinations, edema and livedo reticularis. The chapter's 300–400 mg/day range is not a routine geriatric starting dose (US prescribing information).

old: Peak-dose dyskinesia: reduce levodopa dose, or add amantadine (start 100 mg BID, up to 200 mg BID); buspirone up to 20 mg/day may benefit some patients (p946).
new: For peak-dose dyskinesia, consider smaller levodopa doses or amantadine when appropriate. The chapter describes 100–200 mg twice daily in selected patients (p946). For immediate-release amantadine, tailor initiation and escalation to renal function, age and neuropsychiatric tolerability. The text also describes buspirone up to 20 mg/day in selected patients.

old: Clozapine more effective but agranulocytosis in 1% to 2% → weekly CBC; try quetiapine/pimavanserin first (p946–947).
new: For persistent PD psychosis the chapter considers clozapine after quetiapine or pimavanserin, citing agranulocytosis in 1–2% (p946–947). Follow the absolute neutrophil count: with stable counts, weekly during the first 6 months, every 2 weeks during months 7–12, then monthly (US clozapine labeling).

old: Focused ultrasound (FUS) — FDA-approved 2018 for tremor; ablative/non-programmable, no anesthesia needed (p949).
new: Focused ultrasound creates an irreversible, nonprogrammable lesion. The 2018 US indication was unilateral thalamotomy for medication-refractory tremor-dominant PD. Patients are generally awake, and local anesthetic can be used to secure the stereotactic frame (p949).

old: In PDD motor symptoms precede cognitive symptoms by more than 1 year; in DLB, motor and cognitive symptoms arise within the same year (p939).
new: In PDD, established motor parkinsonism begins more than one year before dementia. Dementia before, together with, or within one year after parkinsonism fits the DLB timing convention (p939, DLB Consortium 2017).

old: In eligible patients, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, with 10% as a bolus and the rest over 1 hour, reduces disability; review hemorrhage risk and exclusions (p966).
new: In eligible patients, IV alteplase is 0.9 mg/kg up to 90 mg total. Give 10% as a bolus over one minute and the remainder over 60 minutes. Review hemorrhage risk and exclusions (p966, Activase prescribing information).

old: McKeith criteria: probable DLB = 2 core features, or 1 core + 1 suggestive feature (p984); exam trap: the text says one core plus one supportive feature and classifies RBD as core, while the Table 63-3 footnote says one core plus at least one suggestive feature and the table classifies RBD as suggestive (p984).Current practice (not the book): probable DLB = ≥2 core features, or 1 core feature + ≥1 indicative biomarker (reduced DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, abnormal MIBG scintigraphy, or PSG-confirmed REM sleep without atonia) — DLB Consortium 4th consensus report (McKeith et al.), 2017.
new: Probable DLB: at least two core clinical features, or one core feature plus an indicative biomarker (DLB Consortium 2017). REM sleep behavior disorder is a core feature. For book questions, p984 discusses RBD as core, while the older Table 63-3 uses the term “suggestive” and places RBD in that category.Current practice (not the book): probable DLB = ≥2 core features, or 1 core feature + ≥1 indicative biomarker (reduced DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, abnormal MIBG scintigraphy, or PSG-confirmed REM sleep without atonia) — DLB Consortium 4th consensus report (McKeith et al.), 2017.

old: "1-year rule": cognitive symptoms must precede parkinsonism by ≥12 months to call DLB vs PDD — arbitrary, often hard to apply (p984).Current practice (not the book): DLB is diagnosed when dementia occurs before or concurrently with parkinsonism; the 1-year rule between onset of dementia and parkinsonism is kept for research DLB-vs-PDD distinction — DLB Consortium (McKeith et al.), 2017.
new: One-year rule: DLB is favored when dementia starts before, concurrently with, or within one year after parkinsonism. PDD is favored when established PD precedes dementia by more than one year. The interval is an operational convention (p984, DLB Consortium 2017).Current practice (not the book): DLB is diagnosed when dementia occurs before or concurrently with parkinsonism; the 1-year rule between onset of dementia and parkinsonism is kept for research DLB-vs-PDD distinction — DLB Consortium (McKeith et al.), 2017.

old: Incidence ~0.6/100,000 person-years (or 1.86–4.9/100,000 population), rising to 6/100,000 person-years after age 50; mean onset 54y; ~3x more common in men (p985).
new: In older epidemiologic studies MSA incidence was about 0.6 per 100,000 person-years, and prevalence was 1.86–4.9 per 100,000 people. The chapter reports incidence rising to 6 per 100,000 person-years after age 50, mean onset at 54 years and a male predominance in its cited population (p985).

old: Orthostatic dx criterion: ≥30 mmHg systolic BP drop (practically, ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic considered significant in the absence of an appropriate heart-rate increase) (p986).
new: In the 2022 MDS criteria, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a systolic fall ≥20 mm Hg, usually accompanied by a diastolic fall ≥10 mm Hg, with a blunted heart-rate response. The time window is 3 minutes for clinically established MSA and up to 10 minutes for clinically probable MSA. The 30-mm Hg systolic threshold on p986 reflects earlier criteria.

old: PPA = isolated language deficit ≥2 years before other decline (p987). nfvPPA: apraxic/agrammatic speech, preserved single-word comprehension; left-dominant atrophy (inferior frontal/insula/caudate); ~20% TDP pathology (usually TDP-43 type A) at autopsy, most show tau (CBD > PSP > Pick) (p988). svPPA: fluent but semantically empty speech, surface dyslexia; begins in amygdala/anterior temporal lobe; most behaviorally prominent PPA; often TDP-43 type C-positive, tau-negative inclusions at autopsy (p988). Logopenic PPA = usually an AD language presentation; may respond to cholinesterase inhibitors if imaging or other biomarkers confirm AD etiology (p987-988).
new: Primary progressive aphasia: insidious, progressive language impairment is the dominant early deficit and the main initial limitation on daily activities. The book describes an older two-year isolated-language criterion (p987). The international consensus criteria do not require waiting two years to diagnose PPA. nfvPPA: apraxic/agrammatic speech, preserved single-word comprehension; left-dominant atrophy (inferior frontal/insula/caudate); ~20% TDP pathology (usually TDP-43 type A) at autopsy, most show tau (CBD > PSP > Pick) (p988). svPPA: fluent but semantically empty speech, surface dyslexia; begins in amygdala/anterior temporal lobe; most behaviorally prominent PPA; often TDP-43 type C-positive, tau-negative inclusions at autopsy (p988). Logopenic PPA = usually an AD language presentation; may respond to cholinesterase inhibitors if imaging or other biomarkers confirm AD etiology (p987-988).

old: Cognitive symptoms must predate parkinsonism by ≥12 months to call it DLB rather than PDD (though this is arbitrary and hard to apply clinically) (p984).
new: DLB can be diagnosed when dementia precedes parkinsonism, begins concurrently, or appears within one year of motor onset. PDD describes dementia after more than one year of established motor PD. The timing convention is described by the DLB Consortium (p984, 2017 consensus).

old: Diagnostic algorithm by symptom count (Fig 65-2, p1011): 1–4 symptoms + functional impairment → "other" (reassurance); 2–4 symptoms + Q1/Q2 + impairment → minor depression (watchful waiting); 3–4 symptoms + Q2 (mood) present 2 years + impairment → chronic depression (probably dysthymia); 5 symptoms + Q1/Q2 + impairment → major depression, graded moderate at PHQ-9 15–19 and severe at PHQ-9 20 (as printed in the table).
new: Figure 65-2 combines symptom count, depressed mood or loss of interest, duration and functional impairment to guide diagnostic assessment. Its chronic-depression row specifies mood symptoms for two years. For standardized PHQ-9 severity, 10–14 is moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, and 20–27 severe (p1011, Kroenke et al.). The score supports evaluation and does not independently diagnose major depression.

old: ECT: response rate >80%, remission rate >60% — no trial has ever shown medications more effective than ECT, and older patients respond even better than younger adults; course is 3–6 treatments/week for 2–4 weeks; few side effects — short-term memory loss almost always resolves within a few weeks (p1014).Current practice (not the book): ECT is typically given two or three times per week; an acute course often consists of 6–12 treatments — American Psychiatric Association (patient page).
new: In studies summarized by Hazzard, ECT response exceeded 80% and remission exceeded 60%, with favorable responses in older adults (p1014). The APA describes an acute course commonly given 2–3 times weekly, often 6–12 sessions. Confusion and difficulty learning new material usually improve, but some autobiographical memory gaps may persist.Current practice (not the book): ECT is typically given two or three times per week; an acute course often consists of 6–12 treatments — American Psychiatric Association (patient page).

old: Most SSRIs, SNRIs, and mirtazapine can be tapered over 2–4 weeks; tricyclics need several months (p1016).
new: Reduce antidepressants in steps, with smaller reductions as the dose falls. Hazzard describes 2–4 weeks for many SSRIs, SNRIs and mirtazapine and longer courses for TCAs (p1016). NICE recommends adjusting the pace to the drug, duration, prior withdrawal and symptoms. Some patients need weeks or months.

old: Fluoxetine is the exception — its long half-life means it does not require tapering, and a single 20 mg dose can even be used to smooth withdrawal from other antidepressants (p1016).Current practice (not the book): fluoxetine can sometimes be stopped by alternate-day dosing at 20 mg/day; at 40–60 mg/day use a gradual withdrawal schedule — NICE NG222 rec 1.4.18, 2022.
new: Fluoxetine has a long half-life. NICE allows a period of alternate-day dosing for some people taking 20 mg/day and recommends gradual withdrawal at 40–60 mg/day. A clinician-directed switch from another drug requires attention to interactions and washout (p1016, NICE NG222 recommendation 1.4.18).Current practice (not the book): fluoxetine can sometimes be stopped by alternate-day dosing at 20 mg/day; at 40–60 mg/day use a gradual withdrawal schedule — NICE NG222 rec 1.4.18, 2022.

old: Moderate: PHQ-9 score 15–19.
new: The validated PHQ-9 grades are 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe and 20–27 severe.

old: Severe: "PHQ-9 score of 20" as printed in the Fig 65-2 table (p1011).
new: Figure 65-2 prints “moderate” for 15–19 and “20” for severe, which differs from the validated severity bands (p1011, Kroenke et al.).

old: Three to six treatments per week for 2 to 4 weeks; ECT has few side effects, and short-term memory loss almost always resolves within a few weeks after the course (p1014).
new: The APA describes two or three ECT treatments per week, often 6–12 treatments, individualized to response. Post-treatment confusion and difficulty retaining new information usually improve. Some memory gaps for events around the treatment period can persist. The chapter gives a different historical frequency (p1014).

old: What tapering schedule applies to most SSRIs, SNRIs, and mirtazapine, and to tricyclic antidepressants?
new: How should antidepressant tapering be individualized, and how does fluoxetine's long half-life affect dose reduction?

old: Which antidepressant is an exception to tapering, and why?
new: Reduce in steps guided by symptoms, half-life and duration of treatment.

old: Most SSRIs/SNRIs/mirtazapine: taper over 2–4 weeks; tricyclics: taper over several months.
new: The book gives 2–4 weeks as an example for several agents and longer tapers for TCAs (p1016).

old: Fluoxetine is the exception — its long half-life means it does not require tapering, and a single 20 mg dose can even smooth withdrawal from other antidepressants (p1016).
new: NICE notes that 20 mg/day of fluoxetine can sometimes be reduced with alternate-day dosing, while 40–60 mg/day requires gradual reduction.

old: US Medicare hospice: attending physician and hospice medical director certify expected prognosis <6 months if the disease follows its usual course; coverage determinations guide prognosis, rather than impose admission requirements. (p. 1046)
new: US Medicare hospice requires a prognosis of six months or less if the illness runs its usual course. Initial certification comes from the hospice physician and, if the patient has a designated attending physician, that physician. Coverage guidelines support clinical judgment (p1046, CMS Medicare Benefit Policy Manual, chapter 9).

old: CDC caution thresholds: reassess benefit/risk >50 MME/day; avoid >90 MME/day (p1060)
new: Before increasing to 50 MME/day or more, pause to reassess benefits and risks and consider precautions. The 2022 CDC guideline for outpatient pain treatment uses dosage as a guidepost and rejects an inflexible 90-MME ceiling. It excludes cancer-related pain treatment, palliative care and end-of-life care (p1060 discusses the 2016 guideline).

old: Gabapentinoids/sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) for neuropathic pain; genotype screening may be indicated for HLA-B*1502 and HLA-A*3101 (most common in South Asian ancestry) — carriers are at risk of severe skin reactions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome; carbamazepine is a potent CYP450 inducer (interacts with warfarin, lithium) (p1065)
new: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are sodium-channel blockers used for selected neuropathic pain syndromes. HLA-B*15:02 increases the risk of SJS/TEN with either drug and is more frequent in several East, Southeast and South Asian populations. HLA-A*31:01 is associated with a broader range of carbamazepine reactions in several ancestries. Carbamazepine induces CYP enzymes and can reduce warfarin exposure. Combined lithium and carbamazepine can cause neurotoxicity (p1065, CPIC).

old: Start at about 25% to 50% of the dose given to younger patients; the CDC recommends carefully weighing risk/benefit above 50 MME/day and avoiding doses above 90 MME/day (p1060).
new: The chapter suggests lower initial opioid doses in older adults, often 25–50% of a younger adult's dose (p1060). Choose the drug and dose for renal function, frailty and prior exposure. CDC 2022 recommends reassessment before reaching 50 MME/day and individualized decisions rather than a fixed 90-MME ceiling.

old: HLA-B*1502 and HLA-A*3101 (most common in South Asian ancestry) — carriers are at increased risk of severe skin reactions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome (p1065).
new: HLA-B15:02 is linked to carbamazepine- and oxcarbazepine-associated SJS/TEN. HLA-A31:01 is associated with several carbamazepine hypersensitivity reactions and occurs across multiple ancestries. The genes do not have the same geographic distribution (p1065, CPIC).

old: Table 75-1 severe cutoffs: AVA < 1.0 cm², velocity > 4 m/s, mean gradient > 40 mmHg (p1150).
new: Severe high-gradient AS: peak velocity ≥4.0 m/s or mean gradient ≥40 mm Hg, with valve area typically ≤1.0 cm². Assess flow and measurement quality when indices disagree. Table 75-1 prints strict inequalities at these boundaries (p1150, ACC/AHA valve guideline).

old: TAVR "prohibitive SAVR risk" = STS Predicted Risk of Morbidity and Mortality > 50% (not STS-PROM/mortality alone); valve durability data only confirmed to 5 years (p1153).
new: The book's prohibitive surgical risk includes predicted one-year death or major morbidity over 50%, together with comorbidities or serious irreversible conditions (p1153). Later randomized NOTION follow-up reported valve outcomes through 10 years in lower-risk patients. Lifetime durability remains uncertain, especially in younger candidates.

old: Table 75-6 tiers — indications (actual replacement criteria): symptomatic + severe AI regardless of LV function, OR asymptomatic + severe AI + EF < 50%, OR severe AI undergoing other cardiac surgery; considerations: asymptomatic, severe AI, normal LV function, dilated ventricle with LVESD > 50 mm, or moderate AI undergoing other cardiac surgery; possible indication: asymptomatic, severe AI, normal function, progressive LV dilatation > 65 mm if surgical risk is low (table does not name the dimension; the text calls it LVESD) (p1155).Current practice (not the book): the 65-mm AR threshold is LV end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD >65 mm, progressive, low surgical risk: may be considered); LVESD >50 mm is the end-systolic trigger — ACC/AHA valvular guideline, 2020.
new: Severe chronic AR: symptoms are an indication for surgery regardless of EF when intervention is appropriate. In asymptomatic patients, the 2020 ACC/AHA threshold for LV systolic dysfunction is LVEF ≤55% without another cause. LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m², and progressive LVEDD >65 mm in selected low-risk patients, represent distinct pathways. Severe AR at other cardiac surgery is an additional indication. Table 75-6 prints an older EF threshold of <50% and lists moderate AR during other cardiac surgery as a consideration (p1155).Current practice (not the book): the 65-mm AR threshold is LV end-diastolic dimension (LVEDD >65 mm, progressive, low surgical risk: may be considered); LVESD >50 mm is the end-systolic trigger — ACC/AHA valvular guideline, 2020.

old: Table 75-7 severe cutoffs: MVA < 1.0 cm², PA pressure > 50 mmHg, mean gradient > 10 mmHg (p1156).
new: Rheumatic mitral stenosis: current ACC/AHA staging defines severe disease at MVA ≤1.5 cm² and very severe disease at ≤1.0 cm². Table 75-7's older echo category “severe” uses MVA <1.0 cm², PA pressure >50 mm Hg and mean gradient >10 mm Hg. Gradient varies with flow and heart rate (p1156).

old: Repair durability, as printed: freedom from reoperation equaling that of valve replacement (7%–10% at 10 years) (p1159).
new: Mitral repair durability: p1159 describes good durability but prints 7–10% as “freedom from reoperation,” an inconsistent endpoint label. In a surgical cohort of 1,604 patients, actual freedom from reoperation after repair was 93.6% at 10 years. Durability depends on anatomy, repair technique and population.

old: Antibiotic prophylaxis (Table 75-14): amoxicillin 2 g PO 1h pre-procedure (standard); penicillin-allergic: clindamycin 600 mg or cephalexin 2 g PO; unable to take oral: ampicillin 2 g IV/IM; unable to take oral + PCN-allergic: clindamycin 600 mg IV or cefazolin 1 g IV/IM (p1161). Given only for gingival/periapical/oral-mucosal dental procedures or active-infection surgery, not routine nondental procedures (p1161).Current practice (not the book): clindamycin is no longer recommended for dental prophylaxis; penicillin-allergic options are cephalexin, azithromycin/clarithromycin or doxycycline PO, or cefazolin/ceftriaxone IM/IV — but no cephalosporin after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin/ampicillin — AHA endocarditis prophylaxis wallet card.
new: Dental endocarditis prophylaxis in adults with eligible high-risk cardiac disease: amoxicillin 2 g orally once, 30–60 minutes before a procedure involving gingiva, periapical tissue or oral mucosa perforation. For penicillin allergy, options include cephalexin 2 g if appropriate, azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg or doxycycline 100 mg. Avoid cephalosporins after penicillin/ampicillin anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria. If oral medication is impossible, the AHA lists ampicillin 2 g IM/IV or cefazolin/ceftriaxone 1 g IM/IV where appropriate. Clindamycin in the historical table is no longer recommended for dental prophylaxis (p1161, AHA prevention wallet card).Current practice (not the book): clindamycin is no longer recommended for dental prophylaxis; penicillin-allergic options are cephalexin, azithromycin/clarithromycin or doxycycline PO, or cefazolin/ceftriaxone IM/IV — but no cephalosporin after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin/ampicillin — AHA endocarditis prophylaxis wallet card.

old: Table 75-15 (INR targets + aspirin): mechanical aortic valve INR 2–3 (2.5–3.5 with risk factors), mechanical mitral valve INR 2.5–3.5 always; bioprosthetic INR 2–3 for 3 months only if no risk factors — with risk factors, bioprosthetic mitral rises to INR 2.5–3.5 (bioprosthetic aortic stays 2–3, no stated 3-mo limit); aspirin 75–325 mg/day with a mechanical valve, 75–100 mg/day with a bioprosthetic valve (p1161).Current practice (not the book): with a mechanical valve on VKA, adding low-dose aspirin 75–100 mg/day for antiplatelet therapy requires a separate indication (ESC/EACTS: concomitant symptomatic atherosclerotic disease) and low bleeding risk; ESC/EACTS 2025 class IIa, level B — ESC/EACTS 2025, Eur Heart J 2025;46:4635; ACC/AHA 2020 class 2b, level B-R — ACC/AHA 2020, Circulation 2021;143:e142.
new: Prosthetic valves: mechanical valves require VKA therapy, with INR target based on valve, position and thromboembolic risk (typically 2.5 for a current-generation mechanical aortic valve without added risk and 3.0 for mechanical mitral valves). US guidance considers VKA to target INR 2.5 for 3–6 months after selected surgical bioprosthetic aortic or mitral replacement. An independent indication may warrant ongoing anticoagulation. Table 75-15 prints an older routine aspirin combination and different bioprosthetic regimens (p1161).Current practice (not the book): with a mechanical valve on VKA, adding low-dose aspirin 75–100 mg/day for antiplatelet therapy requires a separate indication (ESC/EACTS: concomitant symptomatic atherosclerotic disease) and low bleeding risk; ESC/EACTS 2025 class IIa, level B — ESC/EACTS 2025, Eur Heart J 2025;46:4635; ACC/AHA 2020 class 2b, level B-R — ACC/AHA 2020, Circulation 2021;143:e142.

old: Bleeding more likely with INR > 5; INR 5–10: can be treated by holding warfarin + oral vitamin K 1–2.5 mg, check INR daily until < 5 (p1161).Current practice (not the book): INR 4.5–10 with no bleeding: suggest against routine vitamin K; INR >10 without bleeding: oral vitamin K; major bleeding: 4-factor PCC plus vitamin K 5–10 mg slow IV — ACCP/CHEST 9th ed, 2012.
new: Supratherapeutic INR: assess bleeding, urgency and thrombotic risk. Without bleeding at INR 4.5–10, hold warfarin as appropriate and recheck INR. Routine vitamin K is generally unnecessary. The historical option of oral vitamin K 1–2.5 mg at INR 5–10 on p1161 is not a blanket treatment instruction (CHEST).Current practice (not the book): INR 4.5–10 with no bleeding: suggest against routine vitamin K; INR >10 without bleeding: oral vitamin K; major bleeding: 4-factor PCC plus vitamin K 5–10 mg slow IV — ACCP/CHEST 9th ed, 2012.

old: Elective mechanical AV surgery: hold warfarin 48–72 h preop, restart within 24 h postop, no bridging needed if no risk factors; mechanical mitral or aortic valves with high-risk factors are bridged with heparin once INR < 2 (p1162).Current practice (not the book): stop warfarin ≥5 days (rather than <5 days) before an elective surgery/procedure (conditional recommendation) — ACCP/CHEST perioperative antithrombotic guideline, 2022.
new: When warfarin interruption is required for an elective procedure, CHEST generally advises stopping it at least five days beforehand. A bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without added risk generally does not require bridging. For higher-risk mechanical valves, weigh thrombotic and procedural bleeding risks with the valve team. CHEST 2022 suggests against routine bridging, while ACC/AHA allows it in selected high-risk patients. Restart when hemostasis permits (p1162 describes an older 48–72-hour approach).Current practice (not the book): stop warfarin ≥5 days (rather than <5 days) before an elective surgery/procedure (conditional recommendation) — ACCP/CHEST perioperative antithrombotic guideline, 2022.

old: AI surgical trigger is stated twice with different thresholds on the same page: LVESD "> 50 mm" (dilated ventricle, a consideration) vs "> 65 mm" (asymptomatic, low-risk, a possible indication; the table says "progressive LV dilatation", the text says LVESD) — not contradictory once you note these are different tiers of the same table (Table 75-6), but easy to conflate under exam pressure (p1155).
new: In asymptomatic severe AR with preserved EF, distinguish LVESD >50 mm (or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m²) from progressive LVEDD >65 mm in a selected low-risk patient. The narrative on p1155 uses LVESD for 65 mm, while Table 75-6 leaves the dimension unspecified. The 2020 ACC/AHA guideline specifies end-diastolic dimension for the latter threshold.

old: STS Predicted Risk of Morbidity and Mortality > 50%; durability of TAVR valves beyond 5 years is unknown, so some patients may need a reintervention ("valve-in-valve" procedure) (p1153).
new: The historical definition was a predicted one-year risk of death or major morbidity above 50%, taking irreversible comorbidity into account (p1153). Randomized NOTION follow-up now extends to ten years. Very-long-term durability and the feasibility of later valve-in-valve intervention remain patient-specific.

old: At what LVESD threshold should surgery be considered in an asymptomatic, low-surgical-risk patient with severe aortic regurgitation, even without LV dysfunction?
new: In asymptomatic severe aortic regurgitation with preserved LV function, how do LV end-systolic and progressive end-diastolic enlargement affect referral for surgery?

old: LVESD exceeding 65 mm, because of the high risk of sudden death (p1155).
new: LVESD >50 mm or indexed LVESD >25 mm/m² can support surgery. Progressive enlargement into the severe LV end-diastolic range above 65 mm can support consideration in selected low-risk patients. Page 1155 labels this latter dimension differently from ACC/AHA 2020.

old: INR 2–3, for only 3 months after implantation (versus lifelong anticoagulation for a mechanical valve) (p1161).
new: If VKA is chosen after surgical bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement, target INR 2.5 (usual range 2–3). ACC/AHA considers 3–6 months reasonable in selected patients at low bleeding risk. Mechanical prostheses require lifelong VKA, and another indication can prolong anticoagulation with a bioprosthesis (p1161).

old: Held 48–72 hours preoperatively and restarted within 24 hours postoperatively, without heparin bridging, if there are no additional risk factors (p1162).
new: For elective procedures requiring interruption, stop warfarin at least five days beforehand and verify adequate INR decline. A bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without added thromboembolic risk generally needs no heparin bridge. Resume warfarin once hemostasis permits, often within 12–24 hours (p1162, CHEST 2022).

old: Clindamycin 600 mg PO (or cephalexin 2 g PO), given 1 hour before the procedure (p1161).
new: For eligible adults with penicillin allergy, an oral AHA alternative is cephalexin 2 g if there was no anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria, or azithromycin/clarithromycin 500 mg or doxycycline 100 mg. Give one dose 30–60 minutes before the indicated dental procedure. The clindamycin regimen printed on p1161 is historical.

old: Spironolactone — 12.5–50 mg daily; eplerenone — 25–50 mg daily; both contraindicated if creatinine ≥2.5 mg/dL or hyperkalemia; SGLT2 inhibitors reduced death and HF hospitalizations in HFREF in DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced, with similar efficacy over age 75 and regardless of diabetes (p1181).Current practice (not the book): eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m² or serum potassium ≥5.0 mEq/L are contraindications to MRA initiation — AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022.
new: Steroidal MRAs for symptomatic HFrEF: initiate if eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m² and serum K <5.0 mEq/L, then monitor both. The chapter lists spironolactone 12.5–50 mg daily and eplerenone 25–50 mg daily and gives an older creatinine cutoff (p1181). DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced demonstrated improvements in their HF/CV composite outcomes, including in patients without diabetes. Mortality effects differed between trials.Current practice (not the book): eGFR ≤30 mL/min/1.73 m² or serum potassium ≥5.0 mEq/L are contraindications to MRA initiation — AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline, 2022.

old: CRT: NYHA II–IV HFREF, EF ≤35%, QRS ≥150 ms; improves symptoms/survival even in octogenarians, unlike ICD (p1184).
new: CRT: the strongest standard indication includes LVEF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB and QRS ≥150 ms, with NYHA II, III or ambulatory IV symptoms despite guideline-directed therapy. In selected older adults, CRT improves symptoms, quality of life and survival. ICD therapy targets arrhythmic sudden death (p1184, AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022).

old: Only SGLT2 inhibitors show consistent benefit in HFPEF trials to date (p1184).
new: SGLT2 inhibitors reduced HF events in preserved/mildly reduced EF trials. Subsequent FINEARTS-HF also demonstrated a reduction with finerenone in the composite rate of total worsening HF events and cardiovascular deaths among participants with LVEF ≥40% (p1184 describes the earlier evidence).

old: EMPEROR-Preserved (n=5988, EF >40%): death/HF hospitalization HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90, p<0.001), driven by fewer HF hospitalizations; effect consistent regardless of diabetes status (p1188). Dapagliflozin also improved symptoms/exercise function over 12wk in the smaller Preserved-HF trial (n=324) (Table 76-11, p1185).
new: EMPEROR-Preserved: in 5,988 patients with EF >40%, empagliflozin reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for HF (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.90, p<0.001), mainly through fewer HF hospitalizations. Results were consistent regardless of diabetes. PRESERVED-HF, a smaller dapagliflozin trial of 324 patients, assessed symptoms and exercise function at 12 weeks (p1185, 1188).

old: β-blockers: the book says carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, and bisoprolol (the 3 US-approved for HF) are "the only three" proven and "should be used" — but the same page reports SENIORS: nebivolol significantly lowered death/CV hospitalization in patients ≥70 (p1179). Book contradicts itself: pick the 3 for "which β-blockers should be used", but don't reject nebivolol as "no outcome benefit". Metoprolol tartrate is an acceptable titration-phase alternative (p1179).
new: The three guideline-recommended HFrEF beta blockers are carvedilol, metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol. US labeling for bisoprolol alone is for hypertension, although its HFrEF efficacy is established. Among 2,128 patients aged ≥70, SENIORS found a benefit from nebivolol on the composite of death or cardiovascular hospitalization. These are separate evidence and regulatory questions (p1179).

old: Roughly how many Americans are affected by heart failure today, and what is the projected total by 2030?
new: What US heart failure prevalence did Hazzard report, and how many affected adults did the cited projection anticipate by 2030?

old: About 6.5 million today; projected to exceed 8 million by 2030 (p1166).
new: Hazzard reported about 6.5 million US patients and projected over 8 million by 2030 (p1166). Both figures refer to the chapter's reporting period and forecast.

old: What creatinine threshold contraindicates mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone), and what is spironolactone's typical dose range?
new: What renal-function and potassium thresholds govern MRA initiation in HFrEF, and which spironolactone dose range does the chapter describe?

old: Creatinine ≥2.5 mg/dL (or preexisting hyperkalemia); spironolactone 12.5–50 mg once daily (p1181).
new: For MRA initiation in HFrEF, eGFR must be above 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium below 5.0 mEq/L. Monitor both after starting. The chapter describes spironolactone 12.5–50 mg once daily (p1181, AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022).

old: EF ≤35% and QRS ≥150 ms in NYHA II–IV HFREF.
new: The clearest CRT indication is symptomatic NYHA II, III or ambulatory IV HFrEF despite guideline-directed treatment, EF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB and QRS ≥150 ms.

new: CRT can improve function and survival in selected octogenarians. An ICD prevents arrhythmic sudden death (p1184).

new: Which drug class was tested in EMPEROR-Preserved, and which outcome drove the trial's composite benefit?

new: Empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, reduced cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization in EMPEROR-Preserved (n=5,988, EF >40%, HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.90).

new: Fewer HF hospitalizations drove the result, irrespective of diabetes status (p1188).

old: Watchman LAA occlusion: warfarin to INR 2–3 (p1203) for 45 days (p1203) post-implant, then stop if TEE confirms complete LAA closure.
new: WATCHMAN: the original trials used warfarin to INR 2–3 with aspirin for approximately 45 days. Reassessment by TEE looked for device thrombus and significant peri-device leak before transition to antiplatelet therapy. Current postimplant regimens depend on device, bleeding risk, imaging and labeling (p1203).

old: Dabigatran (Pradaxa) 150 mg BID (110 mg BID with concomitant verapamil, age ≥80, or increased GI-bleeding risk) — RE-LY, dose-dependent results: 150 mg → 34% ↓ stroke/SE vs warfarin, similar major bleeding; 110 mg → similar stroke/SE, 20% ↓ major bleeding (p1204, image). Reversal: idarucizumab.
new: Dabigatran. RE-LY studied 150 mg and 110 mg twice daily: 150 mg reduced stroke/systemic embolism by 34% with similar major bleeding to warfarin, while 110 mg had similar efficacy and about 20% less major bleeding. The 110 mg twice-daily AF regimen is jurisdiction-specific (for example, European labeling in selected older patients or with verapamil) and is not the US adult AF dose. Dose by local labeling and renal function. Specific reversal agent: idarucizumab (Table 77-9, p1204).

old: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) 20 mg daily (15 mg if CrCl 30–49) — ROCKET-AF; noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention, but only a similar (not lower) major-bleeding rate vs warfarin (p1204, image). Reversal: andexanet alfa.
new: Rivaroxaban. In ROCKET-AF, 20 mg daily (15 mg for CrCl 30–49 mL/min) was noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention, with a similar major-bleeding rate. US adult AF labeling uses 20 mg with the evening meal when CrCl >50 mL/min, or 15 mg with the evening meal when CrCl ≤50 mL/min within labeled renal-use conditions. US commercial sales of andexanet alfa ended in December 2025. Management of life-threatening bleeding follows local reversal protocols (Table 77-9, p1204).

new: Apixaban for AF: 5 mg twice daily, reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two criteria apply: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL. ARISTOTLE found 21% less stroke/systemic embolism and 31% less major bleeding versus warfarin (Table 77-9, p1205, Eliquis prescribing information).Current practice (not the book): the Eliquis label's weight criterion is body weight ≤60 kg (not <60) — Eliquis prescribing information §2.1 (BMS).

old: Endoxaban / edoxaban (Savaysa) 60 mg daily (30 mg if CrCl 30–50, weight ≤60 kg, or select interacting drugs) — ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48, dose-dependent results: 60 mg → noninferior for stroke/SE, 20% ↓ major bleeding; 30 mg → no stroke/SE benefit (noninferiority margin only, HR 1.07), major bleeding 1.61% vs 3.43% (HR 0.47) vs warfarin (p1205, image).
new: Edoxaban. In the US, adult nonvalvular AF dosing is 60 mg once daily for CrCl >50 to 95 mL/min, or 30 mg once daily for CrCl 15–50 mL/min. Avoid use for NVAF when CrCl exceeds 95 mL/min. Weight and P-gp criteria in Table 77-9 pertain to trial protocols and some other indications or jurisdictions. ENGAGE AF studied higher- and lower-dose strategies, both noninferior for stroke/systemic embolism in its primary analysis, with less major bleeding. The low-dose arm had more ischemic stroke than warfarin (p1205, Savaysa prescribing information §2.1).

old: ICD primary SCD prevention: ischemic CM, LVEF ≤ 35% (p1206) NYHA II–III (or LVEF < 30% (p1206) NYHA I) on GDMT, more than 40 days (p1206) post-MI or more than 90 days (p1206) post-revascularization; or nonischemic CM LVEF ≤ 35% (p1206) NYHA II–III despite GDMT.

Nonischemic cardiomyopathy may qualify with LVEF ≤35% and NYHA II–III despite GDMT. Expected meaningful survival should exceed one year (p1206, AHA/ACC/HFSA).

new: A cardioinhibitory vasovagal response may produce a pause ≥3 seconds or a heart rate <40/min for more than 10 seconds. Dual-chamber pacing may be reasonable in selected patients over 40 with recurrent vasovagal syncope and documented prolonged spontaneous pauses (p1194).

new: The historical regimen used warfarin INR 2–3 with aspirin for about 45 days. Before switching to the planned antiplatelet regimen, assess device-related thrombus and peri-device leak. old: LVEF ≤ 35% with NYHA class II–III (or LVEF < 30% with NYHA class I) on guideline-directed medical therapy, more than 40 days after MI or more than 90 days after revascularization (p1206).
new: After MI, primary-prevention ICD criteria include LVEF ≤35% with NYHA II–III, or LVEF ≤30% with NYHA I, despite guideline-directed therapy and with expected meaningful survival beyond one year. old: AAA means over 50% vessel-diameter enlargement, generally above 3 cm in men. It may remain silent until expansion or rupture (p1214).
new: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is usually defined on ultrasound by an infrarenal aortic diameter ≥3.0 cm or an enlargement at least 50% above the expected diameter. It can remain silent until expansion or rupture (p1214, USPSTF AAA screening recommendation).

old: Repair is generally considered above 5–5.5 cm; endovascular repair has short-term advantages, but long-term outcomes can resemble open repair (p1210).
new: For an unruptured AAA, ACC/AHA recommends repair at a maximal diameter ≥5.5 cm in men or ≥5.0 cm in women. Symptoms attributable to the aneurysm or rapid growth may warrant earlier repair. Endovascular repair can have short-term benefits, with later outcomes dependent on anatomy, follow-up and reintervention (p1210).

old: COPD is currently the 4th leading cause of death in the US; projected to be the 5th leading cause of disability and 3rd cause of death worldwide by 2030 (p1235).
new: Hazzard cited an earlier US mortality ranking and projected COPD to rank fifth for disability and third for death worldwide by 2030 (p1235). In CDC's final 2024 US statistics, the broader category chronic lower respiratory diseases, which includes COPD and asthma, ranked fifth.

old: Half of adults with COPD will be ≥75 years old by 2030 (p1235).
new: The chapter projected that people aged 75 or older would account for about half of adults with COPD by 2030 (p1235).

old: GOLD criterion: fixed FEV1/FVC < 0.70 — doesn't correct for age, overdiagnoses older adults (prevalence 37.7% by GOLD vs 15.4% by age-adjusted Z-score) (p1243–1244).
new: In a compatible clinical context, GOLD uses post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70. Because the fixed ratio does not adjust for age, it can classify more older adults as obstructed than an age-adjusted lower limit of normal. In the older cohort described here, estimates were 37.7% versus 15.4% (p1244, Table 81-5).

old: ATS/ERS FEV1 staging thresholds: ≥70% Pred = mild, 50–69% = moderate, <50% = severe (p1244, Table 81-5).
new: Table 81-5 reproduces older ATS/ERS categories using FEV1 percent predicted: ≥70%, 50–69% and <50% (p1244). The 2022 ERS/ATS interpretive standard grades impairment by z-score. GOLD's airflow-obstruction grades are a separate framework.

old: PRISm = preserved FEV1/FVC ratio but low FEV1 + inflammatory-airway features — still at risk (p1244).
new: PRISm is a post-bronchodilator spirometric pattern with FEV1/FVC ≥0.70 and FEV1 <80% predicted. It can be associated with respiratory symptoms or later airflow obstruction. Demonstrating airway inflammation is not part of its definition (p1244, GOLD).

old: Stepwise approach: SABA rescue → long-acting BD (LAMA usually first-line, greater exacerbation reduction than LABA) → add the other class → add ICS (combined with a LABA — ICS monotherapy is not recommended in COPD, unlike asthma) for frequent exacerbations not controlled by LABA and/or LAMA, hospitalization for exacerbation, or concomitant asthma; ICS+LABA reduces exacerbations/hospitalizations with eosinophils ≥300 cells/mL [sic — the book's own Table 81-7, p1246, gives cells/μL] plus high symptom burden and frequent exacerbations (p1253; agents in Table 81-10, p1249–1252).
new: COPD inhaled treatment: offer a short-acting rescue bronchodilator. GOLD 2026 generally favors LABA/LAMA for symptomatic group B or exacerbation-prone group E patients and considers LABA/LAMA/ICS in group E at eosinophils ≥300 cells/μL. Following exacerbations on LABA/LAMA, ICS benefit is more likely as the eosinophil count rises. Concomitant asthma requires an ICS-containing regimen. Table 81-7 gives cells/μL; the p1253 prose prints cells/mL (Table 81-10, p1249–1252; GOLD treatment algorithms).

old: ICS risks in older adults: 1.2–1.6-fold increased pneumonia risk (highest with older age, frailty, low BMI, high dose, eosinophils <100 cells/mL [sic — the book's own Table 81-7, p1246, gives cells/μL]); ↓ bone mineral density above 1000 mcg/day fluticasone-equivalent; posterior subcapsular cataracts; atypical mycobacterial infection (p1253–1254).
new: ICS risks in older adults: 1.2–1.6-fold increased pneumonia risk (highest with older age, frailty, low BMI, high dose, eosinophils <100 cells/μL); ↓ bone mineral density above 1000 mcg/day fluticasone-equivalent; subcapsular cataracts are established with systemic steroids, while causation with ICS is less certain; atypical mycobacterial infection (p1253–1254).

old: Lung transplant referral thresholds: FEV1/DLCO <25% predicted, PaCO2 >50 mmHg, BODE >5; median post-transplant survival 5–6 years; age >70 has higher 30-day/1-year mortality (p1258–1259).
new: Lung transplant referral thresholds: both FEV1 and DLCO <25% predicted, PaCO2 >50 mmHg, BODE >5; median post-transplant survival 5–6 years; age >70 has higher 30-day/1-year mortality (p1258–1259).

old: ICS combined with LABA reduces exacerbations and hospitalizations with absolute eosinophil count ≥300 cells/mL plus high symptom burden and frequent exacerbations (GOLD Group D).
new: ICS combined with LABA reduces exacerbations and hospitalizations with absolute eosinophil count ≥300 cells/μL plus high symptom burden and frequent exacerbations (GOLD Group D).

new: Pneumonia risk with ICS is greatest with eosinophils <100 cells/μL (also older age, frailty, low BMI, high ICS dose); ICS withdrawal can be considered with eosinophils <300 (especially <100) cells/μL (p1253–1254). new: Atherosclerosis accounts for almost 90% of renovascular cases in older adults (p1287), and a recognized nonatherosclerotic cause is fibromuscular dysplasia; Hazzard prints “fibrous dysplasia” in the paragraph and in Table 83-3 (p1288).

new: Rome IV functional constipation requires at least two features: straining, hard or lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal blockage, manual maneuvers (each in more than 25% of defecations), or fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements/week; criteria must be met during the last 3 months, with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis, rare loose stools without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS (Rome Foundation, C2); Hazzard Table 87-1 prints 12 weeks in the last 12 months (p1354).

old: Telomere shortening begins at age 30 and proceeds at ~1%/year loss; loss of telomere function → genetic instability → oncogenic mutation risk (p1383).
new: Telomeres protect chromosome ends. Their progressive loss can destabilize chromosomes and increase mutation risk. Page 1383 describes a functional decline from age 30 at about 1% per year. Measured leukocyte telomere shortening also occurs in infancy, and its rate varies with age. Human leukocyte study

new: Surgery: healing is compromised at every phase (↓inflammatory/proliferative response, altered collagen); in a retrospective cohort of patients aged 75 or older undergoing cancer surgery, geriatric comanagement was associated with lower 90-day mortality (pp1388–1389). Original surgical cohort

new: Immunotherapy (ICIs): one retrospective cohort observed similar frequencies of high-grade immune-related events by age. new: In one trial of electronic symptom monitoring during treatment, median survival was 31.2 versus 26.0 months. A later community trial found better symptom control, function and quality of life without a survival difference. Symptom monitoring can help even when survival is unchanged (p1391). old: End-of-life nutrition: IV fluids/TPN/tube feeding do not prolong life and may worsen comfort (pulmonary congestion, edema); dehydration near death is generally comfortable except for xerostomia (treat with swabs/ice chips) (p1392).
new: In the last days of life with advanced cancer, routine artificial hydration or nutrition has no established survival benefit and can add edema, pulmonary congestion or procedural burden. Ask about thirst and discomfort, offer mouth care and safe sips or ice chips as tolerated, and individualize decisions with the patient and family (p1392). NCI, Last Days of Life
